questions.q: How does Snowflake's core MERGE INTO ... USING ... ON syntax compare to T-SQL's MERGE?
options: It is nearly identical, including WHEN MATCHED THEN UPDATE/DELETE and WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN INSERT
Snowflake does not support MERGE at all
Snowflake requires a completely different keyword instead of MERGE
Snowflake's MERGE can only insert rows, never update or delete
questions.explain: The core MERGE syntax transfers almost unchanged from T-SQL, including support for multiple WHEN MATCHED clauses with extra conditions.

questions.q: What is missing from Snowflake's MERGE that T-SQL's MERGE supports?
options: An OUTPUT clause to capture affected rows inline
The ability to update rows at all
The USING clause
The ON clause for specifying the join condition
questions.explain: Snowflake's MERGE has no OUTPUT clause — to see what changed, you'd query the target table's Time Travel history separately instead.

questions.q: What is the recommended Snowflake approach for auditing what a MERGE statement changed, given there's no OUTPUT clause?
options: Query the target table's Time Travel history (or CHANGES clause) after the MERGE runs
There is no way to audit MERGE changes in Snowflake
Use the WHEN MATCHED BY SOURCE clause instead
Re-run the MERGE a second time to compare results
questions.explain: Since MERGE itself can't emit affected rows, Snowflake's pattern is to inspect the target table's history via Time Travel or the CHANGES clause after the statement runs.

questions.q: What does Snowflake's WHEN NOT MATCHED clause mean, compared to T-SQL's options?
options: It only means 'in source but not in target' — there is no WHEN NOT MATCHED BY SOURCE equivalent
It means 'in target but not in source', the opposite of T-SQL's default
It behaves identically to T-SQL's WHEN NOT MATCHED BY SOURCE
It cannot be used with INSERT
questions.explain: Snowflake only supports the 'not matched by target' direction (rows present in the source but missing from the target); there's no BY SOURCE / BY TARGET qualifier.

questions.q: How do you delete target rows that no longer exist in the source, since Snowflake's MERGE can't do this in one statement?
options: Run a separate DELETE ... WHERE NOT EXISTS statement against the target table
Add a WHEN NOT MATCHED BY SOURCE THEN DELETE clause to the MERGE
It is not possible to delete such rows in Snowflake at all
Use the OUTPUT clause to trigger the delete automatically
questions.explain: Because Snowflake's MERGE has no BY SOURCE clause, removing target rows that vanished from the source requires a separate DELETE statement using NOT EXISTS (or a similar anti-join).
